title: Your Blazing-Fast Computer Spends Most of Its Life Waiting
subtitle: Yesterday we met the CPU that does billions of things a second. So why is software ever slow? Because the data is stuck in traffic.
hook: We just learned the CPU is a very fast idiot, ripping through billions of instructions a second. So why does *anything* ever feel slow? Here's the secret that separates people who write code from people who make it *fast*: the CPU spends most of its life **waiting** — for data to arrive from memory. And the gap between the fastest and slowest memory isn't 2x. Scaled to human time, it's the difference between **one second and a decade.**

builds_on.label: Your Computer Is a Very Fast Idiot

sections.heading: Memory is a pyramid, not a box
sections.body:
There isn't one 'memory' — there's a **hierarchy**, trading speed for size. Close to the CPU: tiny and instant. Far away: huge and glacial.

- **Registers / L1 cache** — microscopic, basically instant.
- **L2 / L3 cache** — small, very fast.
- **RAM** — gigabytes, but ~100× slower than cache.
- **SSD** — roomy, far slower again.
- **Network / disk far away** — enormous, and painfully slow.

The CPU can only work on data that's *close*. Need something far down the pyramid? It stalls — doing nothing — until it arrives.

sections.label: The gaps, in human time
sections.body: Multiply every real delay by ~a billion so your brain can feel it. **L1 cache = 1 second.** RAM = a couple of **minutes**. An SSD read = a few **days**. A hard-disk seek = **months**. A network hop around the world = **years**. Same clock ticks, wildly different worlds. When code is slow, it's rarely 'too much math' — it's waiting at the far end of this ladder.

sections.caption: Closer to the CPU = faster but smaller. Every step down is a big jump in wait time — which is why *where your data lives* dominates speed.

sections.heading: The trick that saves us: locality
sections.body:
The reason computers aren't hopelessly slow is a habit called **locality of reference**: programs tend to reuse the same data (and data near it) over and over. Hardware bets on this by **caching** — quietly keeping recently-used stuff in the fast tiers.

So the pro move for speed: **keep the data you need close, and touch it in predictable patterns.** Marching through a tidy array is fast (it streams into cache); hopping around chasing pointers is slow (every jump risks a trip down the pyramid). This one idea — mind where your data lives — will come back in caching, databases, and distributed systems all track long.

sections.caption: Computerphile on how CPU caches work and why this whole pyramid exists.

takeaways: A fast CPU is usually **waiting for data**, not out of math.
Memory is a **hierarchy**: registers/cache → RAM → SSD → network, speed traded for size.
The gaps are huge — scaled up, L1 ≈ 1 second while a global hop ≈ years.
**Locality** (reusing recent/nearby data) lets caching hide most of the wait.
Go fast by keeping hot data **close** and access **predictable** — arrays beat pointer-chasing.

quiz.q: If a program feels slow, the usual culprit is…
options: The CPU can't do the arithmetic fast enough
Waiting for data from slower memory tiers
quiz.explain: CPUs are fast at math; the bottleneck is stalling while data travels up from RAM, disk, or the network.

quiz.q: Roughly how much slower is RAM than L1 cache?
quiz.explain: About 100× — seconds vs. minutes on the human-time scale. That's why hot data belongs in cache.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: Yesterday you learned the CPU just loops fetch→decode→execute. How does *that* connect to today?
options: Each loop often stalls waiting to FETCH data from slow memory — that wait is the whole story of speed
The loop runs slower on Tuesdays
quiz.explain: The dumb loop is fast; the slow part is feeding it. Today's lesson is literally 'what the CPU waits for between loops.'

tg_quiz.q: RAM vs L1 cache — roughly how much slower?
tg_quiz.correct: Yep — about 100× slower. Location is everything.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's ~100× slower — seconds vs minutes in human time.
tg_quiz.explain: Which is why caches keep hot data close to the CPU.
